[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 12.0 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"41ed0e","wall_time_seconds":5.3878186,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2685,"output":"27:## Source: sufficient and necessary Assumption ( chain note) (1).pdf\\r\\n29:**Path:** LSAT DUMP/LR/Assumption and Objection Family/Necessary Assumption/Notes/sufficient and necessary Assumption ( chain note) (1).pdf  **Modified:** 2025-07-18T02:45:42.788000+00:00  **Words:** 898  **Doc ID:** None\\r\\n55:Practical Guide to Sufficient Assumption Questions Comprehensive Guide to Sufficient Assumption Questions Using Conditional Logic Simple Example When we think of a sufficient assumption, we\'re considering an unstated premise that, when added to the argument, makes it a valid argument. Essentially, a sufficient assumption guarantees the conclusion when combined with the premises. This means that the premise, when added to the argument, forces the conclusion to follow. Typically, sufficient assump\\r\\n63:Sufficient Assumption. QUESTION STEM KEYWORDS. EXAMPLES. Which of the following if assumed would allow the conclusion to follow logically? The conclusion above is properly drawn if which of the following is assumed? READING GOAL. Find the Conclusion. Find the Support. Ask yourself if theres a new term or idea in the conclusion. (If so that idea needs to be in the correct answer.) Ask yourself what the evidence told us about each half of the conclusion. If there is conditional logic mentally or physically diagram it. Link conditionals together where possible. If there isnt conditional logic try to think of the one way that the conclusion wouldnt be true. The correct answer would need to rule out that possibility. PREPHRASE GOAL. Solve for the correct answer ahead of time. Most of the time were pre-phrasing a conditional idea trying to get from this idea to that idea. The correct answer loves to put that connection in contrapositive form. So if were thinking I need to hear that golfing requires money we remind ourselves that it might sound like if you dont have money you cant golf. CORRECT ANSWER. Which answer when added to the evidence guarantees the truth of the conclusion? Correct answers will do one of these things: Provide the missing link that completes a chain of ideas. Provide the missing fact that triggers a conditional. Rule out the one possible way the conclusion could be wrong. Create a situation where whether X is true or X is false the conclusion is true. WRONG ANSWERS. Right Ideas Wrong Order Illegal negations or reversals of the link we were seeking. Lacks Crucial Term Most commonly this means the answer lacks the undefined New Idea in the conclusion so its powerless to prove that New Idea. Too Weak We have to fully prove the conclusion so some or most usually wont cut it. Stimulus Tendencies. Often shorter arguments with obvious conclusion or premise indicator words. Lots of conditional logic is involved in these arguments. Sometimes math-y stuff. COMMON FORMS. Form 1 A is B. B is C. Thus A is Z. Sufficient Assumption: C is Z. Form 2 A is B. B is C. Thus X is C. Sufficient Assumption: X is A. Form 3 A is B. Y is Z. Thus A is Z. Sufficient Assumption: B is Y. Older versions of Sufficient Assumption were pretty consistent in using verbatim words and phrases multiple times to clearly connect the dots. More modern examples might ask us to equate a word and its definition like seeing possessing more money and property as a match for wealthier or cautiously weighing the evidence before making a decision as a match for prudent. EXAMPLES. Bridge Idea If Premise then Conclusion. Humans are amazing. After all humans invented roller coasters. (SA: invented RCs then Amazing). It is well known that Teslas are the most fuel efficient sports car available. Thus the best sports car available is a Tesla. (SA: most fuel efficient then best). Missing Fact. Only people well-versed with Game of Thrones are invited to Tommys party on Sunday. Thus Shelly must not be invited. (SA: Shelly doesnt know GoT well). If it rains on Thursday then I wont be able to play basketball which was going to be my only exercise this week. Getting at least some exercise every week was my New Years Resolution. So evidently Im not going to be able to keep my New Years Resolution. (SA: its gonna rain on Thursday). Either Carrie or Brad must get coffee for any staff meeting. Since there is a staff meeting tomorrow morning Brad will have to get coffee tomorrow morning. (SA: Carrie cant get the coffee tomorrow). CONDITIONAL CHAINS. Clowns should be excommunicated for scary things are a nuisance and all clowns are scary. (SA: nuisance then should be excommunicated). Buying something impractical requires a firm commitment to having fun. Thus buying a hoverboard is evidence that one is a child at heart since people who are firmly committed to having fun are still children at heart. (SA: hoverboard then impractical). UNIVERSALIZE THE EVIDENCE. We shouldnt accuse Harry of being ungrateful since Thomas behaved in a similar fashion and we didnt accuse Thomas of being ungrateful. (SA: we should judge all cases of ungrateful the same way). Hakeem is a lawyer and he is very verbose. Hence it must be that all lawyers are verbose.\\r\\n71:Defining a Sufficient Assumption. A sufficient assumption is a statement that if added to the evidence guarantees the truth of the conclusion. Its an unstated premise that is enough to prove the conclusion making the argument 100% logically sound. While sometimes called Justify questions this can be misleading. The word justify rarely appears in these question stems and it can also show up in Strengthen questions. Therefore its better to focus on the function of the assumption rather than specific labels. How to Identify Sufficient Assumption Questions. The key is to focus on the verb in the question stem. Look for language that indicates the answer will prove the conclusion. Common Question Stems: The arguments conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed? if which of the following is assumed allows the conclusion to be properly inferred? The conclusion above is properly drawn if which of the following is assumed? if assumed enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn? an assumption that would allow the conclusion above to be properly drawn? an assumption that would serve to justify the conclusion above? Note on Justify: A Sufficient Assumption question asks you to justify the conclusion entirely while a Strengthen question will use softer phrasing like most helps to justify. Strategy for Answering. 1. Reading the Argument. Your initial goal is to break down the argument. Find the Conclusion and the Support. Look for new terms or ideas in the conclusion. This new element must be present in the correct answer to bridge the gap. If the logic is conditional diagram it and link the statements together where possible. If the logic is not conditional think of the one way the conclusion could be false. The correct answer must rule out this possibility. 2. Pre-phrasing the Answer. The goal is to solve for the correct answer ahead of time. You are often looking for a missing conditional link that connects an idea from the premise to an idea in the conclusion. Be prepared for the correct answer to present this link in its contrapositive form. For example if you need the statement Golfing requires money the answer might say If you dont have money you cant golf. Identifying Correct and Incorrect Answers. Correct Answers. A correct answer fully proves the conclusion. It typically does one of the following: Provides the missing link that completes a chain of ideas. Provides a missing fact that triggers a pre-existing conditional rule. Rules out the one possible way the conclusion could be wrong. Common Wrong Answers. Right Ideas Wrong Order: The answer contains the right elements but in an illegal reversal or negation of the required logic. Lacks Crucial Term: The answer choice is missing the new undefined idea from the conclusion which makes it powerless to prove that conclusion. Too Weak: The answer uses words like some or most which are not strong enough to guarantee the conclusion. Common Argument Patterns and Examples. Sufficient Assumption arguments are often short feature conditional logic and may use repeated phrases to connect ideas. More modern tests might equate a word with its definition (e.g. wealthier and possessing more money). 1. The Bridge Idea (If Premise then Conclusion). Argument: Humans are amazing. After all humans invented roller coasters. Sufficient Assumption: If something/someone invented roller coasters then it is amazing. 2. The Missing Fact. Argument: Only people well-versed with Game of Thrones are invited to Tommys party on Sunday. Thus Shelly must not be invited. Sufficient Assumption: Shelly is not well-versed with Game of Thrones. 3. Conditional Chains. Argument: Clowns should be excommunicated for scary things are a nuisance and all clowns are scary. Logic: Clown then Scary then Nuisance. Conclusion: Clown then Excommunicated. Sufficient Assumption: Anything that is a nuisance should be excommunicated. 4. Universalize the Evidence. Argument: Hakeem is a lawyer and he is very verbose. Hence it must be that all lawyers are verbose. Sufficient Assumption: What is true of Hakeem is true of all lawyers.\\r\\n79:SUFFICIENT ASSUMPTION (SA) QUESTIONS Sufficient Assumption questions are like Inference Must be True (MBT) questions, in reverse. In MBT questions, you’re given all the premises and asked to find the conclusion that would make for a valid argument. Here, you’re given the conclusion and all the premises (minus one). You’re asked to supply that missing premise which will make the argument valid. So really, they can easily turn any MBT question into a SA question by switching out the right answer c\\r\\n95:Relevant Question Types Here\'s where conditional diagramming will typically be worth it: - Sufficient Assumption / Principle-Strengthen (stimulus and answers) - Apply the Principle (stimulus) - Parallel / Parallel Flaw (stimulus and answers) - Must Be True / Must Be False (stimulus and answers) Skills to Build Throughout these problems, look for keywords indicating conditional logic. Listen for claims with total certainty, or ones mentioning requirements. Jot down the \\"X → Y\\" version of these cl\\r\\n111:Missing Links inConditional Chains asSuﬃcient AssumptionsBy far the common feature seen on harder SA questions is when the author will present an incomplete conditional argument. The premise or premises will contain a conditional relationship, while the conclusion will also be conditional in nature. What is missing is a portion of the conditional chain. What we have to do is come up with an additional conditional relationship that in conjunction with the conditional relationships in the premises\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"9a68b0","wall_time_seconds":6.2058822,"exit_code":1,"original_token_count":0,"output":""}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 6.8 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"edd605","wall_time_seconds":6.6067465,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":5044,"output":"# Conditional linking: original draft question bank\\r\\n\\r\\nDate: 2026-09-16\\r\\nStatus: authored draft for review. Not installed in the application or published.\\r\\nDesign authority: [Conditional drill input design](2026-09-14-conditional-drill-input-design.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Keep the existing drill and add two kinds of practice\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve paper-first work, five multiple-choice answers, deterministic grading, and the current overall visual style. Add **Supply the missing conditional** and **Must Be True** alongside translation. No argument-repair mode, required diagram builder, handwriting recognition, or long reading-comprehension exercise.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach new mode begins with one worked example, then six symbolic items and four language items. This gives two difficulty ramps: learn the operation with letters, then apply it to wording. Short paragraphs contain only the premises needed for conditional work. They are optional presentation of the same task, not a separate reading mode.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe ten missing-link items below are original sufficient-assumption-style exercises. They are not official LSAT questions. Each asks which ONE supplied option makes the conclusion follow. Other sufficient assumptions can exist outside the choices; the key is not claimed to be the only possible bridge or a necessary assumption.\\r\\n\\r\\nNotation: `¬` means not; `∧` means and; `∨` means inclusive or; `→` means if-then. A, B, C and the other letters name conditions. Answer labels are separate. Parentheses show the complete condition.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Cover the four groups without changing their labels\\r\\n\\r\\nThe 2026-09-15 copy correction requires four groups and a separate “Required means right” takeaway. Preserve the current map:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Group 1: sufficient-side indicators.\\r\\n- Group 2: necessary-side indicators.\\r\\n- Group 3: unless, without, until, except using the appropriate negation operation.\\r\\n- Group 4: no/not-both relationships.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe screenshots also organize ordinary conditional language as rules, universals, guarantees, and requirements. Use these as wording-coverage tags, not replacement numbered groups. Symbolic items assess logic and do not count as evidence of indicator-language mastery. The mixed word items cover all four current groups, but this starter bank does not exhaust every indicator or scenario.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever infer arrow direction merely from the location of a word. For example, “A ensures B” means A → B; the result B follows “ensures.” Unless does not by itself mean exactly one, and no does not always mean negate the same visible noun phrase regardless of sentence structure.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Supply the missing conditional\\r\\n\\r\\nCommon instruction: **Diagram the premises and conclusion on paper. Which additional conditional, if assumed, makes the conclusion follow?** Reveal choices after the paper step. Reveal keys and explanations only after commitment.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML1: Connect the open ends\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. C → D.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: A → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | C → B |\\r\\n| B | D → C |\\r\\n| C | B → C |\\r\\n| D | B → A |\\r\\n| E | D → A |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: C.** Starting with A gets you to B. The second premise starts at C and gets you to D. Add B → C and the chain becomes A → B → C → D.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A joins C to B in the wrong direction. B reverses the second premise. D takes you back to A. E reverses the target rather than establishing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML2: Turn a rule before finding the gap\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. ¬C → ¬B.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: A → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | D → C |\\r\\n| B | C → A |\\r\\n| C | ¬C → D |\\r\\n| D | C → D |\\r\\n| E | D → A |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: D.** Contrapose ¬C → ¬B to obtain B → C. Now A leads to B and then C. C → D finishes the chain.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A runs from the destination back toward C. B loops back to A. C requires ¬C, but the premises give C when A occurs. E begins at D, which is what you still need to reach.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML3: Match the sign as well as the letter\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → ¬B. C → D.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: A → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | B → C |\\r\\n| B | C → ¬B |\\r\\n| C | ¬C → ¬B |\\r\\n| D | D → C |\\r\\n| E | ¬B → C |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: E.** A gives ¬B, not B. The bridge must let you move from ¬B to C. Then C gives D.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A requires B. B and C merely make ¬B a result; neither lets you start from ¬B and reach C. D reverses the second premise.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML4: Work backward from a negative conclusion\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: D → A. B → L.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: ¬L → ¬D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | A → B |\\r\\n| B | B → A |\\r\\n| C | ¬A → B |\\r\\n| D | L → D |\\r\\n| E | A → ¬B |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: A.** Adding A → B creates D → A → B → L. Contrapose the chain: ¬L → ¬B → ¬A → ¬D. That is the conclusion.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: B points across the gap backward. C starts from ¬A, although D supplies A. D reverses D → L. E sends A to ¬B, which does not establish L or exclude D when L is absent.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML5: Supply the second required part\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. (B ∧ C) → D.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: A → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | C → A |\\r\\n| B | A → C |\\r\\n| C | D → C |\\r\\n| D | D → (B ∧ C) |\\r\\n| E | ¬A → ¬C |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: B.** A already gives B. The second rule needs B and C together. Adding A → C supplies C whenever A occurs, so the full trigger is satisfied and D follows.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A does not give C from A. C and D begin with the result you need to prove. E says what happens without A; it says nothing that supplies C when A occurs.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML6: Cover both alternatives\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → (B ∨ C). B → D.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: A → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | D → C |\\r\\n| B | C → A |\\r\\n| C | C → D |\\r\\n| D | A → ¬B |\\r\\n| E | D → A |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: C.** A guarantees at least one of B and C. The B branch already reaches D. C → D makes the other branch reach D too. Either way, A guarantees D.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A and E begin with D. B sends C back to A without ensuring D. D rules out B when A occurs, forcing C, but still gives no path from C to D.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML7: Put the bridge before the existing chain\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: If a visitor\'s badge is scanned, that visitor is admitted. A visitor is admitted only if that visitor\'s registration is current.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: Every invited guest has current registration.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Additional conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | Every visitor whose badge is scanned is an invited guest. |\\r\\n| B | Every visitor with current registration is an invited guest. |\\r\\n| C | No invited guest has their badge scanned. |\\r\\n| D | Every invited guest has their badge scanned. |\\r\\n| E | Every admitted visitor is an invited guest. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: D.** Let G = invited guest, B = badge scanned, E = admitted, R = registration current. The premises give B → E → R. Add G → B to obtain G → B → E → R.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A, B and E make guest status a result, not a starting point that guarantees registration. C blocks the badge condition without ruling out guest status or establishing registration.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1 and 2; rules, universals, requirements.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML8: Link through an incompatibility\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: No expired pass is valid. Entering the facility requires a valid pass.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: Anyone holding only a canceled pass cannot enter the facility.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor this exercise, evaluate the person\'s sole pass. Let C = canceled, X = expired, V = valid, E = permitted to enter using that pass.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Additional conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | Every canceled pass is expired. |\\r\\n| B | Every expired pass is canceled. |\\r\\n| C | Every pass that is not canceled is expired. |\\r\\n| D | Every canceled pass is valid. |\\r\\n| E | Every valid pass permits entry. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: A.** No expired pass is valid means X → ¬V. Entry requires validity: E → V, so ¬V → ¬E. Add C → X and canceled leads to expired, invalid, and therefore no entry using that pass.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: B reverses the needed connection. C addresses passes that are not canceled. D establishes validity rather than excluding entry. E gives another route into the facility, not a reason canceled passes cannot be used.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1, 2 and 4; universals and requirements. The sole-pass condition prevents an unstated second pass from changing the result.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML9: Read “cannot unless” before contraposing\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A shipment cannot leave unless it has been inspected. Inspection guarantees that the shipment is sealed.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: No flagged shipment can leave.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Additional conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | Every unsealed shipment is flagged. |\\r\\n| B | Every flagged shipment is unsealed. |\\r\\n| C | Every flagged shipment is sealed. |\\r\\n| D | Every uninspected shipment is flagged. |\\r\\n| E | Every sealed shipment can leave. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: B.** Let L = can leave, I = inspected, S = sealed, F = flagged. The premises give L → I → S. Therefore ¬S → ¬I → ¬L. Adding F → ¬S establishes F → ¬L.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A reverses the bridge. C supplies a necessary condition for departure without ruling departure out. D makes flagged status a result, not a trigger for being uninspected. E supplies permission to leave rather than preventing it.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1, 3 and 4; guarantees and requirements. All statuses refer to the same decision time.\\r\\n\\r\\n### ML10: Combine alternatives, “no,” and “unless”\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: Every finalist submits a sample or completes an interview. No applicant who completes an interview lacks approval. Applicants receive approval unless a review is pending.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclusion: Every finalist receives approval.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Additional conditional |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | Every applicant without a pending review submits a sample. |\\r\\n| B | Every applicant with a pending review submits a sample. |\\r\\n| C | Every applicant who submits a sample has a pending review. |\\r\\n| D | Every approved applicant submits a sample. |\\r\\n| E | No applicant who submits a sample has a pending review. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: E.** Let F = finalist, S = sample, J = interview, A = approval, P = pending review. The rules are F → (S ∨ J), J → A, and ¬P → A. The interview branch already reaches approval. E supplies S → ¬P, so the sample branch also reaches approval. Both alternatives now support F → A.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A points from no pending review to sample, not from sample to no pending review. B and C connect samples with a pending review, which does not establish approval. D reverses a possible connection from samples to approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1, 3 and 4; universals, OR branches and negation. “Unless” does not say that a pending review necessarily prevents approval.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Must Be True\\r\\n\\r\\nCommon instruction: **Diagram the premises on paper. Which statement must be true if all the premises are true?** A conditional answer states a rule; it does not assert that its trigger actually occurs.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT1: Chain three conditions\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. B → C.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | C → A |\\r\\n| B | ¬A → ¬C |\\r\\n| C | A → C |\\r\\n| D | B → A |\\r\\n| E | C → B |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: C.** A gives B, and B gives C. So A → C. A, D and E reverse valid arrows. B incorrectly treats the absence of A as ruling out C.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT2: Find a connection hidden by contraposition\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. ¬C → ¬B.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | C → A |\\r\\n| B | B → A |\\r\\n| C | A → ¬C |\\r\\n| D | A → C |\\r\\n| E | ¬A → ¬C |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: D.** The second premise contraposes to B → C. Join it to A → B. A and B reverse what is established. C negates the result. E infers from the absence of the starting condition.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT3: Use a negative fact\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → B. B → C. C is false.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | A is true. |\\r\\n| B | B is true. |\\r\\n| C | C is true. |\\r\\n| D | At least one of A and B is true. |\\r\\n| E | A is false. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: E.** ¬C gives ¬B, and ¬B gives ¬A. Here a fact activates the contrapositive chain. Every other option conflicts with the resulting facts.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT4: One part of an AND trigger is already established\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: (A ∧ B) → C. C → D. A is true.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | B → D |\\r\\n| B | A → D |\\r\\n| C | D → B |\\r\\n| D | ¬B → ¬D |\\r\\n| E | D → C |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: A.** A is already established. If B also occurs, both parts of the trigger hold, producing C and then D. B incorrectly treats A alone as enough. C and E reverse arrows. D rules out D merely because this particular trigger is incomplete.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT5: Eliminate one OR alternative\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → (B ∨ C). A is true. C is false.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | B is false. |\\r\\n| B | B is true. |\\r\\n| C | C is true. |\\r\\n| D | Both B and C are true. |\\r\\n| E | A is false. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: B.** A guarantees at least one of B and C. C is ruled out, so B must hold. A rejects the remaining alternative. C and D conflict with ¬C. E contradicts the stated fact A.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT6: Different branches, same result\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: A → (B ∨ C). B → D. C → D.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | D → A |\\r\\n| B | A → B |\\r\\n| C | A → D |\\r\\n| D | A → C |\\r\\n| E | ¬A → ¬D |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: C.** Either available branch reaches D. You do not need to know which branch occurs. A reverses the resulting rule. B and D select one alternative without support. E rules out D when A is absent, even though D could occur another way.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT7: Combine “every” and “only”\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: Every editor reviews submissions. Only certified staff review submissions.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | Every certified staff member is an editor. |\\r\\n| B | No person who is not an editor is certified. |\\r\\n| C | Everyone who reviews submissions is an editor. |\\r\\n| D | Every editor is certified. |\\r\\n| E | Every certified staff member reviews submissions. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: D.** Editor → reviewer. “Only certified staff” makes certification necessary for reviewing: reviewer → certified. Therefore editor → certified. A, C and E reverse established connections. B infers not certified from not editor.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1 and 2; universals and requirements.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT8: Chain through a “no” rule\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: No damaged package is accepted. Every insured package is accepted.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | No insured package is damaged. |\\r\\n| B | Every undamaged package is insured. |\\r\\n| C | Every uninsured package is damaged. |\\r\\n| D | Every accepted package is insured. |\\r\\n| E | Every damaged package is insured. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: A.** Damaged → not accepted. Contrapose: accepted → not damaged. Insured → accepted → not damaged. B and D reverse valid relationships. C treats not insured as enough to establish damage. E connects damage to insurance without support.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 1 and 4; universals and contraposition. Universal rules do not establish that any packages actually exist.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT9: Chain “unless” with “only if”\\r\\n\\r\\nPremises: The machine operates unless the safety switch is off. The machine operates only if cooling is active.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | If the safety switch is off, the machine does not operate. |\\r\\n| B | If cooling is not active, the safety switch is off. |\\r\\n| C | If cooling is active, the machine operates. |\\r\\n| D | If the machine does not operate, the safety switch is not off. |\\r\\n| E | If cooling is not active, the safety switch is not off. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: B.** Let S = switch off, O = operates, C = cooling active. The premises give ¬S → O → C. Contrapose the chain: ¬C → ¬O → S. A adds an unwarranted converse to the unless rule. C reverses the cooling requirement. D and E negate the switch condition incorrectly.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: Groups 2 and 3; requirements. Treat these as stipulated rules about the same operating state, not a claim about real machinery.\\r\\n\\r\\n### MBT10: A short mixed-premise paragraph\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery research grant requires approval. Approval is withheld unless the review is complete. No incomplete application receives a completed review. A completed review guarantees either a standard award or an exception. This application receives a research grant but does not receive a standard award.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich statement must be true about this application?\\r\\n\\r\\n| Choice | Statement |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A | It receives an exception, and it is incomplete. |\\r\\n| B | It receives no exception, and it is complete. |\\r\\n| C | It receives a standard award, and it is complete. |\\r\\n| D | Its review is not complete, and it receives an exception. |\\r\\n| E | It receives an exception, and it is complete. |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Answer: E.** Let G = grant, A = approval, R = completed review, K = complete application, S = standard award, E = exception. Diagram G → A → R. The no rule is ¬K → ¬R, so R → K. The guarantee is R → (S ∨ E). The grant establishes R and K. Since S is false, E must hold. Both parts of choice E follow.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhy the others fail: A contradicts the application\'s completeness. B denies the required remaining award alternative. C contradicts the stated absence of a standard award. D contradicts the completed review established by the grant.\\r\\n\\r\\nCoverage: all four map groups across universal wording, requirements, unless and no; guarantees; contraposition; OR elimination. Application completeness and review completeness are deliberately distinct conditions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Small changes to the drill screen\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Keep the existing visual identity and paper-first step. Put the premises in a compact numbered stack. In missing-link mode, separate the target conclusion with a short divider. In Must Be True mode, show only the question until choices are revealed.\\r\\n2. Use a small mode label: Translate, Missing conditional, Must Be True. Show progress within a short set, such as 3 of 10. Keep the front page largely intact.\\r\\n3. Show exactly five authored choices with exactly one correct option for these new modes. Keep extra explanation expandable so the screen does not show several competing answer panels.\\r\\n6. Keep original attempt, retry and revealed answer distinct in saved history. ## assistant

Minimal future wiring:

- Keep **one Conditional Reasoning entry** in the Activity Centre; open a small hub with General Conditionals, Linking, Missing Link, and optional separate Must Be True.
- Preserve existing General Conditionals assignment URLs and content. Its hub tile opens the current runner, retaining progress.
- Add a static hub route alongside `/activities/sections`, protected by `has_activity_access`. Existing routes are in [App.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/App.tsx:476).
- Change only the conditional entry’s destination in [ActivityCentre.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/pages/ActivityCentre.tsx:117). Keep distinct activity/run IDs behind the hub’s tiles.
- Avoid renaming the underlying existing activity as a shortcut: [registry.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/worlds/registry.tsx) currently derives its world binding from its title. Use stable IDs for new navigation.

Notation is a **new user-directed requirement**, not an established renderer in this checkout. Current conditional choices display `NOT`, while whiteboard parsing uses `¬`. The draft’s slash-negated letters, written **and/or**, and unbracketed diagrams should govern the future display renderer.

No app files changed.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 13.2 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"757bec","wall_time_seconds":6.6026377,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":661,"output":"# Context Map\\r\\n\\r\\nThe repo has more than one bounded context, each with its own language. This map points to where each glossary lives.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Contexts\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Public surface](./src/pages/CONTEXT.md) — the unauthenticated landing + sign-in page (`Auth.tsx`): how LSAT U describes itself to a prospective student.\\r\\n- [Teacher workspace](./src/pages/teacher/CONTEXT.md) — Joshua\'s admin operator surface (`/teacher`): assigning prepared material to students and the transcript pipeline.\\r\\n- [Teacher Desk page](./src/pages/teacher/desk/CONTEXT.md) — the named visual regions of the desk page itself (the boxes on screen), nested under the teacher workspace. Names the layout so we can revise it precisely.\\r\\n- [Guided Drills & Explanations](./src/components/drill/CONTEXT.md) — the practice domain: guided drills, the question bank, drill instruction cards, and per-question explanations (the Phase 2 authoring work).\\r\\n- [Classroom](./src/components/classroom/CONTEXT.md) — the student\'s own room: the Classroom frame, its sections, and the flag-versus-wrong-answer distinction.\\r\\n- [Reading Comprehension](./src/features/rc/CONTEXT.md) — full-passage RC drilling: passages, sessions, attempts, reveal modes, status, and the adaptive picker.\\r\\n- [Activity Centre](./src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md) — coach-led skill exercises a student is assigned, and the Read, Recall, Colour drill that runs inside one: Chunk, Detail, Coverage, The Recall, Report Card.\\r\\n- [Booking](./src/components/booking/CONTEXT.md) — paying for and scheduling tutoring time: Packages, Booking Passes, the public microsite, and the Single Session (Slots, Holds, Bookers).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Relationships\\r\\n\\r\\n- Both surfaces describe the same product but to different audiences (prospective student vs. operator), so a word can carry different weight in each. Check the right glossary before reusing a term.\\r\\n- A **flag** (Classroom) and a **wrong answer** (Wrong Answer Journal) are different things on different tables: a flag is chosen mid-question, a wrong answer is earned by missing one. Never collapse the two, and never let \\"flagged\\" drift into meaning \\"struggled with\\".\\r\\n- **Set** now means one thing everywhere: the group a student assembles and drills. It used to mean a passage\'s position within its section in Reading Comprehension; that sense is now called **Position** (the data still carries `setNumber`). The collision was retired when the LR and RC pickers merged into one surface — a primary noun that changed meaning when you flipped the mode was the confusion the merge existed to remove. See `docs/adr/0006-rc-selection-is-question-grain.md`.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"4a2edb","wall_time_seconds":6.2537234,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":656,"output":"1:# Activity Centre\\n3:The home for bespoke, coach-led skill exercises (e.g. Negation Station) that a student is assigned and works through conversationally. Distinct from the question-bank MCQ **Drill** engine: Activities are authored content with their own answer keys, not timed runs over `qid` questions.\\n7:**Activity Centre**:\\n11:**Activity**:\\n17:_Avoid_: LSAT U landing page, Foyer, Activity Centre list\\n28:Reserved term. The existing question-bank engine: a timed run over multiple-choice questions pulled by `qid`. An Activity is NOT a Drill.\\n47:**Activity assignment**:\\n53:The four-step vocabulary of the RRC runner, plus the language its grading uses.\\n84:What a stimulus\'s Read turns on, in the judge\'s and the card\'s shorthand: the loophole, inference or conflict the argument runs on. Always defined on a surface before it is used, because \\"you found the move\\" means nothing to a student reading it for the first time.\\n100:Delivering a stimulus as a flat run of facts rather than a story in her own words. The opposite failure to Reciting: Coverage looks perfect and the argument was never held together.\\n111:**Attempt**:\\n112:One complete run of one section by one student. A section may be attempted any number of times, and every Attempt keeps its own date, its own recording and its own Report Card. Nothing is overwritten and nothing is hidden once done.\\n113:_Avoid_: Try, retry, session (reserved for a tutoring session), run\\n125:The page a student meets before a section run, and the parts of it that carry\\n126:names. Nothing here is a phase of the runner; these are things drawn on one\\n130:The page a student lands on before running an RRC section: the method as four Beats, her last few Attempts, and the one control that starts the run. `SectionLaunch` in code, `.sl-` in CSS. It replaces the editorial intro for section mode only; the eight typed Activities keep theirs.\\n131:_Avoid_: The Chamber (the approved mockup\'s name for it, and already a world under `worlds/chamber/`), Homepage (that is an Activity\'s own intro page), intro, splash, lobby, dashboard\\n138:One mark in the row that draws a past Attempt: one per stimulus slot, placed at its authored `item_order` rather than its array position. Four states, because three would lie — `recorded`, `notJudged` (the judge never answered, so the mark is hollow), `silent` (she spoke nothing into that stimulus), `missing`.\\n142:The clock the section was meant to fit, taken from the assignment\'s time goal at her resolved accommodation. Distinct from the question-bank MCQ **Drill** engine: Activities are authored content with their own answer keys, not timed runs over `qid` questions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Language\\r\\n\\r\\n**Activity Centre**:\\r\\nThe module that hosts and lists Activities. The student\'s home for assigned skill work that isn\'t question-bank drilling.\\r\\n_Avoid_: Activities Centre, Skills Centre, Drill Centre\\r\\n\\r\\n**Activity**:\\r\\nOne bespoke skill exercise — a titled, self-contained set of authored items with an answer key, worked through with a coach (e.g. \\"Negation Station\\"). The unit a teacher assigns.\\r\\n_Avoid_: Skill drill, drill (reserved for the MCQ engine), station, module, game\\r\\n\\r\\n**Homepage**:\\r\\nJoshua-facing shorthand for an individual Activity\'s intro/start page: the page that shows the Activity title, item count, overview copy, example, and Start action before the student begins the first Question Set.\\r\\n_Avoid_: LSAT U landing page, Foyer, Activity Centre list\\r\\n\\r\\n**Question Set**:\\r\\nCodex-facing term for one complete per-question unit inside an Activity: the Question Type, the prompt, the response area, the coach feedback, the credited answer, and the answer key material used to judge the response. In the UI, this should still be labeled \\"Question N\\"; when Joshua says \\"question set,\\" he means this full unit, not the collection of all questions.\\r\\n_Avoid_: Question collection, drill set, item bank\\r\\n\\r\\n**Question Type**:\\r\\nThe classification pill inside a Question Set that names what kind of statement or reasoning form the student is working with (e.g. \\"Universal Statement,\\" \\"Conditional Statement,\\" \\"Causal Statement\\"). This is the canonical term for the label currently shown above the prompt.\\r\\n_Avoid_: Category, tag, badge, label\\r\\n\\r\\n**Drill**:\\r\\nReserved term. The existing question-bank engine: a timed run over multiple-choice questions pulled by `qid`. An Activity is NOT a Drill.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Item**:\\r\\nOne prompt within an Activity that the student responds to (e.g. a single statement to negate). | Term | Established meaning | Implication for proposal |
|---|---|---|
| **Activity** | A titled, self-contained collection of authored items and answer keys; the unit a teacher assigns. Glossary line 11. | General, Linking, Missing Link, and MBT can be four Activities grouped beneath one hub. |
| **Activity assignment** | Per-student issued snapshot of an Activity, with progress and score; immutable content once issued. Line 47. | Preserve existing General assignments. Adding sibling Activities must not rewrite their snapshots. |
| **World** | The visual surface replacing the runner’s left column and intro cover, without owning submission, grading, progression, or persistence. Defined by [ADR 0009](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/docs/adr/0009-read-recall-colour-is-a-runner-not-a-world.md:17). | “Four worlds” is compatible as user-facing imagery, but technically four practice destinations are not automatically four `WorldBinding`s. The hub is a navigation/launch surface. |
| **Attempt** | Under the **RRC-specific** section: one complete section run by one student, retaining its date, recording, and Report Card; repeatable without overwriting. Glossary line 111. | Do not silently apply this recording-specific definition to conditionals. Typed activity history needs an explicitly defined complete-practice attempt distinct from each answer submission. |
| **Run** | No independent general Activity definition. In RRC’s Attempt entry, “run” is explicitly an avoided synonym. | Draft terminology currently needs normalization; a practice sitting and a within-question retry must not share one ambiguous label. |

Material contradictions/gaps:

- The glossary still describes Conditional Rephrase’s former free-text local parser at line 40. That description is stale relative to the settled multiple-choice direction.
- **“Question Set” means one complete per-question UI unit**, not a bank or ten-question practice collection, at line 19.
- The existing technical **World** contract concerns presentation, while the proposed hub divides learning content and progress. Use separate Activity identities and define their relationship to the hub; decide themed world presentation separately.
- Calling these “drills” in conversation is harmless user language, but the glossary reserves **Drill** for question-bank MCQs. Student navigation can simply use the four concrete names.
- The glossary does not yet define a conditional hub, activity family, or typed repeat-practice attempt. These are new domain concepts, not existing terms whose behavior can be assumed.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 15.7 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"7bd823","wall_time_seconds":3.9085164,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":512,"output":"---\\r\\nname: grilling\\r\\ndescription: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any \'grill\' trigger phrases.\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nInterview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.\\r\\n\\r\\nWork the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven\'t heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user\'s answers before the next round.\\r\\n\\r\\nFormat a round like so:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\n❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\\r\\n\\r\\n➡️ <your recommended answer>\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>\\r\\n\\r\\n➡️ <your recommended answer>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nEach round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.\\r\\n\\r\\nFinding _facts_ is your job, never the user\'s. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it; don\'t ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don\'t block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user\'s: put each to them and wait.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"f39111","wall_time_seconds":3.4264167,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":852,"output":"---\\r\\nname: domain-modeling\\r\\ndescription: Build and sharpen a project\'s domain model. Use when discussing codebase terminology, writing or editing a CONTEXT.md, or recording or editing an ADR.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Domain Modeling\\r\\n\\r\\nActively build and sharpen the project\'s domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that\'s a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you\'re changing the model, not just consuming it.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## File structure\\r\\n\\r\\nMost repos have a single context:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\n/\\r\\n├── CONTEXT.md\\r\\n├── docs/\\r\\n│   └── adr/\\r\\n│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md\\r\\n│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md\\r\\n└── src/\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\n/\\r\\n├── CONTEXT-MAP.md\\r\\n├── docs/\\r\\n│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions\\r\\n├── src/\\r\\n│   ├── ordering/\\r\\n│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md\\r\\n│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions\\r\\n│   └── billing/\\r\\n│       ├── CONTEXT.md\\r\\n│       └── docs/adr/\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## During the session\\r\\n\\r\\n### Challenge against the glossary\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. \\"Your glossary defines \'cancellation\' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### Sharpen fuzzy language\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. \\"You\'re saying \'account\': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### Discuss concrete scenarios\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Cross-reference with code\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: \\"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### Update CONTEXT.md inline\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don\'t batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Offer ADRs sparingly\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly offer to create an ADR when all three are true:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful\\r\\n2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder \\"why did they do it this way?\\"\\r\\n3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons\\r\\n\\r\\nIf any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. ## assistant

**A new cloud migration is required for student-owned repeated conditional practice.** Existing APIs cannot safely create these runs. This is verified from repository schema, not live deployed schema.

Existing persistence:

- `recordItemResponse(input)` and `listItemResponses(assignmentId, studentId)` in [activitiesClient.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/api/activitiesClient.ts:186) support assigned item submissions.
- Response uniqueness is **assignment_id + student_id + item_order + attempt_no**: [migration](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/supabase/migrations/20260823140000_activity_item_responses_one_row_per_attempt.sql:31).
- `ActivityRunner` reconstructs progress from those rows, treating `attempt_no` as retries within an item. Reusing higher numbers for repeat sessions would break replay and scoring.
- Preview and practice reruns deliberately bypass writes at [ActivityRunner.tsx:488](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/components/ActivityRunner.tsx:488).

Permissions:

- Students can select/update their own assignments, but **cannot insert assignments**.
- Admin assignment insert requires `public.has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin')` **and** `assigned_by = auth.uid()`.
- Assignment snapshots are immutable to non-admin users, including items, title, instructions, activity ID, attribution, and creation time. [Assignment migration](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/supabase/migrations/20260614100100_create_activity_assignments.sql:29).
- Response SELECT permits owner or admin. Response INSERT checks only `auth.uid() = student_id` in the original policy, not ownership of the referenced assignment. Do not copy that weaker relationship check into the new design. [Response migration](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/supabase/migrations/20260614100200_create_activity_item_responses.sql:26).

Existing creation paths are unsuitable:

- `startSectionAttempt(activityId)` calls `start_section_attempt`, which explicitly rejects activities whose mode is not `section`. It also abandons prior runs and deletes empty ones, contrary to typed resume and preservation requirements. [RPC migration](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/supabase/migrations/20260903240000_a_run_is_graded_once_and_an_abandoned_one_never.sql:100).
- `useAssignActivity` calls `assignWork`, which **always sends notifications**, even when the wrapper receives `notify:false`. Do not use it for silent practice creation. [useAdminActivities.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/hooks/useAdminActivities.ts:106).
- Static activities can render using a synthetic preview assignment, but that creates no durable assignment or run.

Recommended bounded migration:

- Add **`conditional_practice_runs`**, separate from original teacher assignments.
- Include client-generated UUID, owner ID, stable activity key, content version, complete immutable question/choice snapshot, status, cursor, responses/reveal state, timestamps, and revision.
- Owner-scoped SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE; INSERT requires owner = `auth.uid()`. Restrict updates so ownership, identity, and original content snapshot cannot change. Admin read only if required for teacher history.
- Direct owner writes are reasonable for self-practice data, whose grading is already client-side. Do not represent these records as tamper-proof examinations.
- Use revision compare-and-swap for state updates. Direct update with `.eq("revision", expected)` plus returned-row checking can avoid an RPC, provided the revision transition and immutable fields are enforced appropriately. An RPC is cleaner if atomic transition validation is needed.
- Client-generated submission IDs and immutable per-submission records within the saved run prevent duplicate retries. Retain original answer separately from later corrections.
- Preserve original General assignments and their first-run history; link new runs to the originating assignment when applicable, without mutating it.

This avoids new Edge Functions. It still requires deploying the SQL migration through the authorized Lovable route. Browser-local persistence alone cannot fulfill cross-device saving.

## assistant

Implemented General session persistence in isolated checkout.

- Own preview and repeats create separate saved snapshots.
- Resume restores paper stage, selection, attempts, feedback, position, completion.
- Explicit reveal is distinct from exhausting attempts.
- Missing sessions show errors; viewing another student writes nothing.
- Original scores and completed history remain intact.
- Added optional `paperReady` / `onPaperReady` to `PaperDiagramPanel`.

Validation: **27 focused tests passed** across practice, redrill, resume, admin view. Typecheck found store errors already reported to you; runner enum error fixed.

Changed: `ActivityRunner.tsx`, `PaperDiagramPanel.tsx`, `ActivityRunner.redrill.test.tsx`, new `ActivityRunner.practice.test.tsx`. No commits or deployment.

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"@'\nimport { useState, type ReactNode } from \"react\";\nimport { ArrowLeft, ArrowRight } from \"lucide-react\";\nimport { ConditionalScene } from \"./ConditionalScene\";\nimport \"./drill-entrance.css\";\n\ntype DrillMode = \"general\" | \"linking\" | \"missing-link\" | \"must-be-true\";\ntype DemoStep = 0 | 1 | 2;\n\ninterface EntranceStep {\n  title: string;\n  detail: string;\n  caption: string;\n}\n\nconst instructions: Record<DrillMode, readonly [EntranceStep, EntranceStep, EntranceStep]> = {\n  general: [\n    {\n      title: \"Diagram the statement\",\n      detail: \"Read it once. Put the sufficient condition on the left and the necessary condition on the right.\",\n      caption: \"If P, then Q. P is enough to guarantee Q.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Choose the matching diagram\",\n      detail: \"Open the choices and look for the diagram that expresses the complete statement.\",\n      caption: \"P leads to Q. Seeing Q alone does not establish P.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Check the direction\",\n      detail: \"Check your answer, then read the explanation before moving on.\",\n      caption: \"The contrapositive reverses the order and negates both conditions: without Q, there is no P.\",\n    },\n  ],\n  linking: [\n    {\n      title: \"Map the premises\",\n      detail: \"Diagram the premises and the conclusion on paper.\",\n      caption: \"Start with P leading to Q. The conclusion needs a path from P to R.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Find the connection\",\n      detail: \"Choose the conditional that connects the premises to the conclusion.\",\n      caption: \"Q leading to R connects the end of the premise to the end of the conclusion.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Follow the whole chain\",\n      detail: \"Check your answer to see why the completed chain reaches the conclusion.\",\n      caption: \"P leads to Q, and Q leads to R. So P leads to R.\",\n    },\n  ],\n  \"missing-link\": [\n    {\n      title: \"Locate the gap\",\n      detail: \"Read the premises and the conclusion. Mark where the chain stops.\",\n      caption: \"P leads to Q, and R leads to S. To establish P leading to S, the middle needs a connection.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Supply the missing rule\",\n      detail: \"Choose the conditional that makes the conclusion follow.\",\n      caption: \"Q leading to R supplies the missing connection. R leading to Q would run it backwards.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Test the completed chain\",\n      detail: \"Check your answer and trace each step from the premise to the conclusion.\",\n      caption: \"P leads to Q, Q leads to R, and R leads to S. The chain now guarantees P leading to S.\",\n    },\n  ],\n  \"must-be-true\": [\n    {\n      title: \"Map what you know\",\n      detail: \"Diagram the given statements on paper.\",\n      caption: \"The premises say P leads to Q and Q leads to R.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Follow what is guaranteed\",\n      detail: \"Choose the answer that must be true whenever those statements are true.\",\n      caption: \"Following both arrows gives P leading to R. No extra premise is needed.\",\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Check the inference\",\n      detail: \"Read the explanation and check why the answer follows from the premises.\",\n      caption: \"P guarantees R. text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"@'\nfrom pathlib import Path\np=Path('src/features/activity-centre/worlds/switchyard/diagramChoices.ts');s=p.read_text().replace('  routes: DiagramRoute[];\\n  responseText:', '  routes: DiagramRoute[];\\n  /** Explicit second half of a paired answer; absent on historical single diagrams. */\\n  contrapositiveRoutes?: DiagramRoute[];\\n  translationCorrect?: boolean;\\n  contrapositiveCorrect?: boolean;\\n  responseText:')\ns=s.replace('export function buildPaperDiagramChoices(', 'export function buildLegacyPaperDiagramChoices(')\ns+='''\n/**\n * Grade the two labelled answers separately against the original statement.\n * Combining them into one truth table would let a bad half be hidden by a\n * stronger other half, especially on a biconditional.\n */\nexport function buildPaperDiagramChoices(creditedAnswers: string[], itemOrder: number): PaperDiagramChoice[] {\n  const direct = parseRoutes(creditedAnswers[0] ?? \"\");\n  if (!direct) return [];\n  const atoms = [...new Set(direct.flatMap(route => [route.ifSide.text, route.thenSide.text]))];\n  const creditedSignature = diagramSignature(direct, atoms);\n  // The converse of a biconditional is correct. Choose a real semantic error,\n  // retaining every clause rather than making shorter options into a clue.\n  const wrong = [reverse(direct), changeOneSide(direct), invert(direct)].find(routes =>\n    diagramSignature(routes, atoms) !== creditedSignature);\n  if (!wrong) return [];\n  const validContrapositive = flip(direct);\n  const wrongContrapositive = flip(wrong);\n  const pairs = [\n    { id: \"paired-correct\", routes: direct, contrapositiveRoutes: validContrapositive,\n      feedback: \"Both parts match the statement. The contrapositive swaps the conditions and negates each complete condition.\" },\n    { id: \"paired-translation-only\", routes: direct, contrapositiveRoutes: wrongContrapositive,\n      feedback: \"The diagram matches the statement, but the contrapositive does not. Swap the conditions and negate each complete condition.\" },\n    { id: \"paired-contrapositive-only\", routes: wrong, contrapositiveRoutes: validContrapositive,\n      feedback: \"The contrapositive matches the statement, but the first diagram changes the rule. Check its direction and polarity against the original statement.\" },\n    { id: \"paired-neither\", routes: wrong, contrapositiveRoutes: wrongContrapositive,\n      feedback: \"These two parts agree with each other, but both change the original statement. First check the translation, then derive its contrapositive.\" },\n  ];\n  return shuffled(pairs.map(pair => {\n    const translationCorrect = diagramSignature(pair.routes, atoms) === creditedSignature;\n    const contrapositiveCorrect = diagramSignature(pair.contrapositiveRoutes, atoms) === creditedSignature;\n    return {\n      ...pair, translationCorrect, contrapositiveCorrect,\n      verdict: translationCorrect && contrapositiveCorrect ? \"correct\" as const : \"partial\" as const,\n      responseText: `Diagram: ${diagramResponseText(pair.routes)} Contrapositive: ${diagramResponseText(pair.contrapositiveRoutes)}`,\n    };\n  }), itemOrder);\n}\n''';p.write_text(s)\n'@ | python -","workdir":"C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-conditional-update",login:false,max_output_tokens:1000}));
